description_full: Sysco Corporation, through its subsidiaries, engages in the sale, marketing, and distribution of food and related products to restaurants, healthcare and educational facilities, lodging establishments, and other foodservice customers. It operates through U.S. Foodservice Operations, International Foodservice Operations, SYGMA, and Other segments. The company distributes frozen food, such as meats, seafood, fully prepared entrées, fruits, vegetables, and desserts; canned and dry food; fresh meats and seafood; dairy and beverage products; imported specialties; and fresh produce. It also supplies paper products, including disposable napkins, plates, and cups; tableware comprising glassware and silverware; cookware consisting of pots, pans, and utensils; restaurant and kitchen equipment and supplies; and cleaning supplies. The company operates in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Sweden, and internationally. Sysco Corporation was incorporated in 1969 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.
ceo_bio: Mr. Brandon Elliot Sewell | Executive VP & CFO | Age 45 | Compensation: $956,259 (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 75K people. Revenue per employee of $1.1M ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Defensive peers, with revenue growing 5%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $26K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Sysco Corporation is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $38.0B market cap on $84.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 7% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.9B in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.50× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.6×.

Shareholder yield of 3.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Slow-motion taste and channel shifts — private label, Gen-Z health preferences, or a DTC disruption can erode decade-old brand moats without a single dramatic quarter.
Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sector_tailwinds: Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
38 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Consumer Defensive sector showing strong relative momentum, outperforming the market by 10% over 3 months
Consumer Defensive ETF in a sustained uptrend above its long-term average

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.45x its revenue share).
It accounts for 2.5% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+13.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 8% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 8% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.57, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.09 vs 5y 0.50), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $231.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 63% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 43% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 12% below its DCF fair value of $87.68, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $66.62 to $118 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 6% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 5.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 12 covering analysts target $91.25 on average, 18% above the price.
The price implies 2.5% annual cash-flow growth, 3pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 6.8% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It runs a 18% gross margin and converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.50x.
ROE of 66% is amplified by 10.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.1% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.6x net debt to EBITDA ($1.8B of cash against $12.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.6x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.3, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.5% over 3 years, 10.5% over 5 years and 5.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 4.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.2% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (0.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 6.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 87%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase, net $192K bought).
It returns 3.3% a year to shareholders (0.5% in buybacks and 2.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 2.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 75,000 employees, each generates about $1.1M of revenue, 2.2x the Consumer Defensive median, and revenue has grown 5.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $26K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $956K (1x revenue per employee).
